concepts.title: Kiko and the Bouncing Drum
concepts.impossibleRule: Every time Kiko hits the drum, it bounces him upward; each successive hit sends him higher.
concepts.extraordinaryOpening: Kiko is already airborne above the floor in surprise, just after striking the toy drum directly beneath him.
shortBeatSummary: 0–2s: Kiko hits the drum once and is already lifted into the air in surprise.
2–5s: He lands and hits again; the second bounce is higher.
5–8s: The drum shifts or rolls slightly; Kiko follows and accidentally keeps triggering more bounces.
8–11s: Kiko stops hitting, thinks the bouncing is over, and relaxes.
11–15s: As he settles, his hand lightly taps the drum; the same rule triggers one final, larger bounce. Hard cut while he is airborne.
concepts.strength: The cause and effect can read immediately, with a strong airborne first frame, clear escalation, expressive reactions, and a simple final payoff.
concepts.mainRisk: Impact timing must visibly connect each drum hit to Kiko’s bounce; the drum must not appear to launch him by itself.

productionPackage.conceptSummary: Kiko discovers that every time he strikes a toy drum, it bounces him into the air—and each new hit sends him higher. He tries again, follows the slightly rolling drum, then relaxes when the bouncing seems to stop. A small accidental tap triggers one last, biggest bounce, ending on Kiko’s surprised face in midair.

beatPlan.beat: Begin mid-action: Kiko has just struck the drum and is already airborne above it, eyes wide. Within the first half-second, show the drumhead rebound and Kiko continue upward so the hit-to-bounce rule reads clearly.
Kiko lands beside the drum, gives it a deliberate second palm strike, and springs noticeably higher than before.
The same drum rolls a short distance. Kiko follows and makes two quick accidental palm taps while catching up; each tap gives him a higher, readable bounce.
Kiko stops touching the drum, lands safely, watches it settle, and relaxes with a relieved little smile. Hold the calm briefly.
As Kiko settles beside it, his hand lightly taps the drumhead. The established hit rule sends him into one final, biggest bounce. End on his delighted, surprised face in midair with a hard cut.

productionPackage.firstFrameImagePrompt: Create one vertical 9:16 first frame for a family-friendly, high-quality 3D animated preschool short. Show Kiko, a cute four-year-old child, already airborne above the playroom floor in a clear mid-action pose. Directly beneath him is one small toy drum, large and unobstructed enough to read instantly. Kiko’s open palm is just lifting away from the slightly compressed drumhead after a strike; his bent knees, lifted feet, upward body motion, wide eyes, and surprised open-mouth expression make it immediately clear that the drum hit has just bounced him into the air. Keep Kiko and the entire drum together in a close-medium full-body composition, with enough floor visible to judge his height. Clean, warm indoor playroom, simple uncluttered background, soft cheerful lighting, appealing polished 3D animation. One child, one drum, one continuous clear physical gag. No other toys, props, people, text, subtitles, logos, motion streaks, or visual clutter. Use the official Kiko character reference if supplied; preserve its design exactly. If no verified Kiko reference is supplied, keep the design simple and consistent without inventing signature identity details.
productionPackage.motionVideoPrompt: Create a 15-second vertical 9:16 family-friendly 3D animated short starring one cute four-year-old child, Kiko, and one toy drum. Preserve Kiko’s supplied canonical appearance throughout; do not invent or change identifying features. Use a stable, locked close-medium full-body camera in one simple indoor playroom, keeping Kiko, the entire drum, and enough floor visible at all times. Start already mid-action: at frame zero Kiko is airborne just above the drum after a palm strike. Within the first 0.5 seconds, clearly show the drumhead rebounding and Kiko moving upward, so viewers understand that the hit caused the bounce. Keep the physics readable and playful, with safe soft landings. The single impossible rule is: every time Kiko hits the drum, it bounces him upward, and each successive hit sends him higher. Follow this timing: 0–2s, first hit and surprised first bounce; 2–5s, Kiko lands, deliberately hits again, and bounces higher; 5–8s, the same drum rolls only a short distance, Kiko follows and accidentally taps it twice, each hit causing a higher bounce; 8–11s, he stops touching it, lands, watches it settle, and relaxes briefly; 11–15s, as he settles, his hand lightly taps the drumhead, triggering the same rule and one biggest final bounce, then hard cut on his surprised, delighted face while airborne. Keep the rhythm brisk, with a clear action or reaction every one to two seconds and a short calm pause before the final surprise. Make every drum contact visibly precede its corresponding bounce. The drum never launches Kiko without contact, moves by itself, duplicates, transforms, or gains a second power. Keep one Kiko, one drum, one room, and the same camera and lighting. No extra characters or objects, no text, no cuts before the final hard cut, no camera movement, no body distortion, no unsafe impact, and no long idle reaction.
essentialRiskNotes: The drum contact must visibly precede every bounce, especially the first one within 0.5–1.0 seconds.
Bind and verify Kiko’s canonical visual reference before image generation; the character registry confirms his name, not his visual design.
Keep the drum’s short roll and the camera framing controlled so both Kiko and the drum remain readable.

concepts.title: Kiko and the Upward-Flowing Juice
concepts.impossibleRule: Whenever Kiko tilts the cup to drink or pour a sip, the orange juice flows upward against gravity and returns to that same cup instead of reaching him.
concepts.extraordinaryOpening: Kiko is thirsty and already tipping his transparent orange-juice cup toward his mouth when the juice curves upward and returns to the cup instead of reaching him.
shortBeatSummary: 0–2s: Thirsty Kiko immediately tries to drink; the juice rises away from his mouth and returns to the tilted cup.
2–4s: He tips the cup farther to get a sip; the ribbon rises into a taller arc and returns.
4–6s: He adjusts the cup toward his lips and tries again, but the same rule sends the juice back into the cup.
6–8.5s: He tries to pour a sip into his open palm as another way to drink; the inverted cup still pulls the juice back upward.
8.5–11s: The inverted cup remains full and his palm dry. Kiko is still thirsty; he turns the cup back to his mouth for one last attempt as the juice returns to the cup. Hard cut.
concepts.strength: A strong, immediately visible visual anomaly.
concepts.mainRisk: Liquid simulation may look inconsistent or obscure the simple rule.

productionPackage.conceptSummary: Thirsty Kiko wants to drink his orange juice, but every time he tips the cup to sip or pour, the juice flows upward against gravity back into the same cup. He tries different ways to get a sip, ending with an inverted cup that remains full and Kiko still thirsty.
productionPackage.singleImpossibleRule: Whenever Kiko tilts the cup to drink or pour a sip, the orange juice flows upward against gravity and returns to that same cup instead of reaching him.
productionPackage.objectConvention: One transparent cup with its juice; the liquid stream is part of that cup/object action, not a second prop.

beatPlan.beat: IMMEDIATE SIP ATTEMPT: Kiko is thirsty and wants to drink his orange juice. At frame zero he is already bringing the tilted transparent cup to his mouth for a sip. The juice instead curves upward against gravity and returns through the same cup opening, away from his lips. He pauses, surprised, still trying to drink.

TRY A BIGGER TILT: To get a sip, Kiko tips the cup farther toward his mouth. The same juice ribbon rises into a taller arc and returns to the cup instead of reaching him. The attempt clearly escalates but still serves the same goal.

REALIGN FOR A SIP: Kiko adjusts the cup opening directly toward his lips and tries again. The same ribbon climbs upward and returns into the cup; no juice reaches his mouth. He reacts with thirsty disbelief.

TRY TO CATCH A SIP: As another way to drink, Kiko places his open palm under the opening and turns the cup completely upside down above it, expecting to catch juice in his hand. The juice still curls upward into the same inverted cup; his palm stays dry.

GOAL-RELATED PAYOFF: The continuous ribbon rapidly retracts into the inverted cup, which remains visibly full. Kiko sees his dry palm and realizes he still has not had a sip. Still thirsty, he turns the cup back toward his mouth for one last attempt; the juice curls back into the cup again. Hard cut on the full cup and Kiko’s still-thirsty, astonished face.

productionPackage.firstFrameImagePrompt: 0-2s: Create one polished family-friendly 3D animated first frame in vertical 9:16. Use the supplied approved Kiko visual reference and preserve his official face, hairstyle, proportions and clothes exactly. Kiko is thirsty and is already bringing one transparent cup of orange juice toward his mouth to take a sip. The cup is visibly tilted for drinking. At frame zero, one thick, glossy, asymmetric ribbon of orange juice is already visibly curving UPWARD against gravity away from his lips and returning through the opening into the same cup. Make it obvious the juice refuses to reach him. Show the complete cup-to-ribbon path clearly beside Kiko’s eager, surprised face. Bright, simple playroom, locked close-medium composition, phone-screen readability. Exactly one child, one transparent cup, and one continuous juice ribbon. No additional props, people, text, logos, splashes, droplets, closed ring or fountain shape.
productionPackage.motionVideoPromptModel: OpenArt Seedance 2.0 Mini; image-to-video; 11s; 480p; 9:16; one locked camera; no generation requested.
productionPackage.motionVideoPrompt:
Create an 11-second vertical 9:16 family-friendly polished 3D animated short. Preserve Kiko’s official appearance, one transparent cup of orange juice, the simple playroom and a stable close-medium camera. Kiko’s clear everyday goal throughout is to drink his orange juice. Exactly one impossible rule: whenever he tilts the cup to drink or pour a sip, the juice flows upward against gravity and returns into that same cup instead of reaching his mouth or hand. Every major action must be a logical attempt to get a sip; do not stage physics demonstrations unrelated to drinking. Keep the orange ribbon continuous, fluid and visibly connected to the cup. No additional magic, objects, characters, splashes, text or camera cuts.

0.0–2.0s — OPENING: Kiko is thirsty and wants to drink his juice. Start already mid-action with the tilted cup at his mouth and the orange juice visibly rising away from his lips before returning through the same opening into the cup. He pauses in surprise but keeps trying.
2.0–4.0s — BIGGER ATTEMPT: Kiko tips the cup farther toward his mouth to get a sip. The same ribbon rises into a taller arc and returns to the cup, still out of reach.
4.0–6.0s — REALIGN: He adjusts the opening directly toward his lips and tries again. The same rule sends the juice upward back into the cup; no sip reaches him. His thirsty disbelief grows.
6.0–8.5s — ALTERNATE WAY TO DRINK: Kiko places his open palm under the opening and turns the cup completely upside down, hoping to catch a sip in his hand. The same ribbon curls back upward into the inverted cup; his palm remains dry.
8.5–11.0s — PAYOFF: The stream rapidly retracts into the inverted cup, which remains visibly full. Kiko sees his dry palm and realizes he is still thirsty. He turns the cup toward his mouth for one last attempt; the juice returns into the cup again. Hard cut on his thirsty, astonished face and the full cup. The ending directly shows the unresolved consequence of his goal.

Keep the stream thick, smooth, connected and entirely inside the locked frame; do not add separate droplets, splashes or extra streams.

passedRules.message: Sufficient consequence variety: 5 distinct consequences.

details.recommendation:
Before writing a 15-second prompt, verify that the core mechanic
can naturally generate at least 4 visually distinct consequences.

If it cannot, reject the concept.

Do NOT stretch a two-beat teaching contrast into 15 seconds.

passedRules.message: Good visual state distribution. Max state: 22.7%.

details.recommendation:
No single visual state may occupy more than approximately
25–30% of the entire video unless meaningful new physical
consequences occur within that state.

Different dialogue or tiny movements do NOT count
as different visual beats.

passedRules.message: Good action variety. Max repetition: 1.

details.recommendation:
The same physical action should not repeat more than twice
unless each iteration introduces a materially different consequence.

Emotional variation (confused → understanding → frustrated)
without physical consequence change is insufficient.

passedRules.message: No explicit cycles detected.

details.recommendation:
A cause-effect cycle (action → consequence → reset) should not
repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

Example cycle: sharpen → draw → blunt → (reset to sharpen)

Cosmetic variations (stroke pattern, sharpen duration) do not
count as structural escalation.

passedRules.message: Good novelty distribution. Max gap: 2.5s.

details.recommendation:
New consequences should be distributed across the timeline,
not clustered at the beginning or end.

No gap longer than 4.5 seconds should pass without a new
visually distinct consequence appearing.

passedRules.message: Good novelty timeline. Static pattern: 0.0%.

details.recommendation:
No more than 50% of the video should pass without new
visually distinct physical consequences appearing.

If > 65% of video shows only pattern variations of the same
core action, flag as CRITICAL.

passedRules.message: Final payoff at 8.5s. Consider moving earlier for stronger retention.

details.recommendation:
The final major escalation should not appear after 80% of the video
(12 seconds in a 15-second video) unless the middle contains
strong intermediate escalations.

Late payoffs risk losing viewer attention before the peak.

passedRules.message: Final payoff is distinct from opening.

details.recommendation:
The final beat must not be identical or nearly identical
to the opening beat.

A callback is acceptable if it's BIGGER or has a TWIST.
A simple repeat signals lazy structure.

passedRules.message: Overall complexity: high. Render uncertain. Consider simplifications.

details.recommendation:
Prompts marked as "very_high" complexity should not proceed
to render without human review and risk acceptance.

Very high complexity typically means 4+ simultaneous high-risk
operations or untested novel requirements.

details.recommendation: The problem must already be visually obvious within the opening second, with no setup, narration, or text explanation required. hook.startsMidAction must be true and hook.visualStrength must be at least 4/5. RULESET 1.3 adds a tolerance window -- hook.startsAt must be <= 0.8s (defaults to 0.0 when absent, a no-op for pre-1.3 IRs); the anomaly doesn't need to be literally frame-0 to read as immediate.

passedRules.message: No stalled progression. Longest motionless beat: 0.0s.

details.recommendation: No beat may hold with motionAmount == 'none' for longer than 1.5 seconds. Renamed from "No Dead Air" in RULESET 1.3 -- brief stillness (a puzzled look, a short charming reaction) is a legitimate pause, not a defect; what matters is progression not stalling, not motion itself.

passedRules.message: 0 main props, within the short-tier budget of 2.

details.recommendation: Introduce the minimum number of props necessary. setting.mainProps count must not exceed 2 for short-tier videos, 4 for long-tier videos. RULESET 1.3 adds a timeline-aware check (heuristic, text-match based) alongside the static count -- a prop first mentioned mid-concept inside an attempt beat, rather than established from the opening, is flagged as a WARNING even when the total count is within budget.

passedRules.message: No fake-resolution beat found. This is a bonus, not a requirement — consider adding a moment where the problem appears solved before the twist.

details.recommendation: Bonus (non-blocking): at least one beat with consequenceType == 'fake_win' before finalPayoff.startsAt, giving the audience a moment to believe the problem is solved before the final twist.

passedRules.message: Longest detached stretch: 0.0s, within tolerance.

details.recommendation: While the core problem is actively unresolved (at least one attempt beat has occurred, final payoff not yet started), no consecutive stretch of beats.relatesToCoreProblem == false may exceed 0.5 seconds. Brief transitions/reaction beats under that threshold are not flagged; only a genuine abandonment of the active problem fails.

passedRules.message: Final payoff salience (7) ties the earlier peak. Acceptable but not ideal — consider making the ending strictly the peak.

details.recommendation: The final payoff's beat.intensity should be at least as high as the highest intensity seen earlier in the video. Computed independently from beat.intensity values; finalPayoff.isPeakIntensity is never trusted as the verdict, only cross-checked for discrepancy reporting. Optimization-level (WARNING), never a blocker. Renamed from "Final Peak Intensity" in RULESET 1.3 -- "intensity" read as motion/chaos, but beats[].intensity is a 1-10 visual/emotional energy scale; a quiet, conclusive beat can score as high as a frantic one.

passedRules.message: Ordinary hard-cut ending, no loop claimed. Fully valid.

details.recommendation: A retention-optimization dimension, never a hard blocker. A strong natural loop back to the opening (finalPayoff.loopsToOpening + loopQuality == 'strong') is a bonus. An ordinary hard cut with no loop claim is fully valid (neutral PASS). Only specific weak-ending text patterns (fade-out, 'the end', walks away) with neither a loop nor a hard cut produce a WARNING-severity FAIL.

details.recommendation: Deterministic companion to ATTEMPT_002: flags a dominant primaryVerb ROOT across attempts (e.g. PUSH / PUSH_HARDER / PUSH_FROM_LEFT all share the root PUSH) even when full verb labels are distinct and ATTEMPT_002's LLM duplicate-strategy check already passed. Catches 'more activity, not a new strategy' in the gray area between CHAR_002 (time-active) and ATTEMPT_002 (label/semantic distinctness). No LLM call.

details.recommendation: Fills the gap between PRODUCIBILITY_001 (very-high-complexity hard block) and PRODUCIBILITY_002 (prop count budget): a middle tier of AI-generation risks (precision alignment, cloth/rope simulation, liquids, thin dangling objects, face/hair contact, multi-object stacking). Uses a tag-based diagnostic model (riskTags in evaluation details) rather than one rule per risk type. Deterministic substring match against setting.mainProps and beat action/consequence text, no LLM call. Always CRITICAL when any tag is found — a human-review trigger, not an outright render block.

attempts.reason: The beat contains a concrete action/result pair without a known high-risk tag.

details.recommendation: Distinct from ATTEMPT_002 (semantic strategy diversity): ATTEMPT_002 asks whether the character is genuinely trying a different strategy; this asks whether that different strategy will actually LOOK different and be reliably executable by an image-to-video generation model (e.g. Seedance). A deterministic keyword pre-filter flags abstract-intent language ('blocks the escape route', 'tries to outsmart') and vague movement-magnitude phrasing ('slightly moves') on attempt beats, plus a beat-budget estimate (too many attempts for the available duration). An LLM semantic check (check_attempts_are_generation_executable) judges each attempt for a concrete action-result pair and flags attempts that would visually collapse into the same choreography despite different wording. BLOCKER only when NO attempt is judged executable at all or the LLM is unreachable (SERVICE_ERROR); CRITICAL when some attempts are unexecutable or abstract-intent language is matched; WARNING for vague magnitude phrasing or beat-budget pressure alone.

concepts.title: Kiko and the Car That Drives on the Wall
concepts.impossibleRule: The car prefers vertical surfaces and escapes back to the wall whenever Kiko tries to bring it down.
concepts.extraordinaryOpening: The toy car is already driving or parked on the wall instead of the floor.
concepts.shortBeatSummary: The car drives higher on the wall; Kiko tries to bring it down; it returns to the wall, climbs toward the ceiling, and escapes to another vertical surface as Kiko reacts.
concepts.strength: The impossible surface preference is immediately readable.
concepts.mainRisk: Wall and ceiling continuity may break as the car crosses surfaces.

concepts.title: Kiko and the Self-Building Block Wall
concepts.impossibleRule: Whenever Kiko removes or pushes blocks, the wall instantly rebuilds or grows.
concepts.extraordinaryOpening: A block wall has already built itself between Kiko and the thing he wants.
concepts.shortBeatSummary: Kiko removes blocks; the wall rebuilds; he pushes it and it grows; he tries to go around it; the wall relocates and closes him off again.
concepts.strength: The obstacle and its escalating consequences are easy to understand.
concepts.mainRisk: Many blocks can create visual clutter and make the main action hard to read.

concepts.title: Kiko and the Chair That Won’t Let Him Sit
concepts.impossibleRule: Whenever Kiko tries to sit, the chair slides away and repositions itself.
concepts.extraordinaryOpening: Kiko is already in a sitting pose as the chair slips out from under him.
concepts.shortBeatSummary: Kiko tries to sit; the chair slides away; he chases and jumps for it; it escapes again; he fakes resting; the chair makes one final slide-away.
concepts.strength: The action is simple to stage and easy to follow.
concepts.mainRisk: The opening is less extraordinary than the other candidates.

editorialRanking.strength: The upward-flowing juice is the clearest and most distinctive frame-zero anomaly; the cup orientation, failed sip and full inversion create a varied escalation and a readable final reveal.
editorialRanking.risk: Continuous liquid shape and cup-orientation continuity are high Seedance risks; mitigated in the prompt with one thick ribbon, one cup, no splashes and locked framing.

editorialRanking.strength: A toy car driving on a vertical wall is immediately understandable and uses one simple rule.
editorialRanking.risk: The existing beat summary repeats pursuit/return, offers a weaker final payoff, and requires consistent small-object tracking on the wall.

editorialRanking.strength: A self-building wall creates a clear obstacle and has room for escalation.
editorialRanking.risk: Many individual blocks create clutter and count/continuity risk; rebuilding, growth and relocation blur the single rule.

editorialRanking.strength: Single chair and simple movement are comparatively feasible to animate.
